title: The O2
data_source: O2’s name and customers, AEG’s arena
hook: A phone network turned a national joke into the world’s most popular music venue.
situation: The Millennium Dome had become a national embarrassment. AEG was reopening it as an entertainment venue and needed a partner, and O2 wanted something that would keep its customers loyal.
exchange: O2 put its name on the venue and built its customer offer around it. Customers got Priority Tickets before anyone else, and the venue got a famous name from day one.
brought: Its name, millions of customers and the money to market the venue.
A reopened arena and a programme of the biggest acts in music.
turning_point: The O2 opened in 2007. In its first seven months it drew 3.4 million visitors, generated £61m worth of PR, and a million O2 customers signed up for Priority Tickets.
measure: Return on marketing investment in the 2010 IPA paper, based on £639m of projected profit from new customers
evidence: Two IPA papers track the sponsorship. The first, in 2008, reported a 26:1 return a year after launch. The second, a Gold in 2010, projected a £639m contribution to profit from new customers over the communications’ lifetime. Both are O2’s own models, written up for an effectiveness award.
lesson: Don’t badge a venue, build your customer offer into it. The 2010 paper calls this breathing rather than badging.
take: The benchmark every sponsorship pitch I have seen gets measured against. It worked because the customer got something real, not just a logo on a roof.

title: A New Kind of Airline
hook: Rival airlines agreed to sell themselves as one network.
situation: Frequent business travellers wanted to fly anywhere on one ticket and one loyalty scheme. No single airline could cover the world.
exchange: Each airline brought its routes, lounges and loyalty members. Together they offered a network none could offer alone.
brought: Routes, lounges, loyalty schemes and planes.
One brand and one promise to travellers across all of them.
turning_point: Star Alliance launched in 1997. Advertising ran in airports and business titles, and some planes were repainted to match.
metric_label: Partner airlines by the time of the IPA paper
measure: The number of member airlines described in the 2000 IPA paper
evidence: The IPA paper reports that the advertising built awareness and a preference for flying within the network among frequent international travellers. That is tracking evidence, not a sales model.
lesson: Competitors can be partners when the customer’s problem is bigger than any one of them.
take: The most unusual partnership in this edition: rivals agreeing to share a brand. It only works because travellers cared more about the network than the logo.

title: Big Brother 2
data_source: BT Cellnet’s phones, Big Brother’s viewers
hook: A TV sponsorship that turned into a mobile business.
situation: BT Cellnet wanted to be familiar and relevant to 16 to 24 year olds. Big Brother was the show they were all watching.
exchange: BT Cellnet paid £4m to sponsor the second series. It also made the show something viewers could follow and take part in on their phones, around the clock.
brought: Sponsorship money and a mobile network for updates and votes.
The biggest young audience on British television.
turning_point: In 2001 the sponsorship went beyond the idents. Viewers could follow the house by mobile, and BT Cellnet earned money from the traffic.
measure: Incremental revenue reported in the 2002 IPA paper, alongside over £10m in media value
evidence: The IPA paper reports £880,000 in incremental revenue and more than £10m of media value. The revenue alone didn’t cover the fee, so the case rests on the brand benefits too.
lesson: A sponsorship can pay for part of itself if you give the audience something to do through your product.
take: An early sign of where sponsorship was heading. The money came from participation, not the idents.
credit: IPA 2002 · Silver · PHD Media for BT Cellnet
deal_value: £4m sponsorship fee, as stated in the IPA paper

title: 1 Pack = 1 Vaccine
stage: Launched and measured for the cause
hook: Every pack of nappies paid for a vaccine.
situation: Maternal and newborn tetanus was killing babies in dozens of countries. Pampers wanted parents to see it as more than a nappy.
exchange: For each specially marked pack sold, Pampers funded a tetanus vaccine through UNICEF. In Ireland, for example, that meant €0.078 a pack.
brought: Packs in millions of homes, and money per pack.
Vaccination programmes, and trust with parents.
turning_point: The campaign began in 2006 and ran for years across many markets. By 2014 it had helped provide 300 million doses of tetanus vaccine.
measure: Doses of tetanus vaccine the partnership helped fund, per a 2014 announcement. By 2021 UNICEF credited it with nearly a million newborn lives saved
evidence: The outcome for UNICEF’s side is well documented in partner releases and UNICEF’s own material. No public figure shows what the partnership did for Pampers’ sales or share.
lesson: A cause partnership is easiest to trust when the exchange is simple enough to fit on the pack.
take: The clearest proof in the edition is for the charity, not the brand. That’s the right way round, but it means Pampers’ own return stays private.
announcement: Read the ten-year story · UNICEF Ireland

title: Party Like a Celeb
hook: A frozen food chain sponsored the jungle, and sold Christmas party food.
situation: Iceland needed better sales over Christmas in a tough market. Its customers, many of them mums, loved I’m a Celebrity.
exchange: Iceland sponsored the show and hired ‘Queen of the Jungle’ Kerry Katona as its ambassador. The show got a sponsor whose campaign ran in step with it.
brought: Sponsorship money and a party food range.
A huge winter audience and a celebrity it had made famous.
turning_point: The ‘Party Like a Celeb’ campaign tied Iceland’s party food to the show through the Christmas season.
metric_label: Sales of the party food range
measure: Growth in party food sales reported in the IPA paper, with payback of over £1.20 for every £1
evidence: The IPA paper reports a 26% rise in party food sales and a payback of more than £1.20 per £1 spent. That is a modelled return on the campaign.
lesson: Sponsor what your customers already love, and sell them the product that fits the moment.
take: Not glamorous, and very effective. The sponsorship worked because the audience and the shoppers were the same people.

brand: Elephant Chakki Gold × South Asian TV
title: Go for Gold
data_source: A flour brand, primetime shows on ethnic channels
hook: A flour brand sponsored the shows its customers watched, on a £28,000 budget.
situation: South Asian families in the UK wanted to eat more healthily, but saw healthy flour as less tasty. Elephant Chakki Gold, a wholegrain flour that looks like white flour, had very little money to spend.
exchange: The brand sponsored popular primetime programmes on key South Asian channels, alongside one TV advert. The channels got a sponsor that spoke to their audience.
brought: A healthier flour and a tiny budget.
Primetime shows trusted by the communities the brand wanted to reach.
turning_point: In 2008 the sponsorships put the brand in front of the families it wanted, show after show.
metric_label: Growth rate achieved, per the IPA paper
measure: The brand’s growth rate reported in the IPA paper, on a campaign budget of £28,000
evidence: The IPA paper reports 206% growth on a very small budget. It doesn’t publish a model separating the sponsorship from other factors in the summary, so it counts as a sales trend.
lesson: Small brands can partner precisely. Choose the channel your customers trust, not the biggest one you can afford.
take: The smallest budget in the archive so far, and one of the biggest growth rates. Proof that partnership is a tool for challengers, not just giants.
credit: Mediareach Advertising for Elephant Chakki Gold

title: 4Homes
hook: When DIY sales collapsed, B&Q sponsored the nation’s home makeover shows.
situation: DIY sales fell sharply in 2008. B&Q needed to inspire people to improve their homes when money was tight.
exchange: B&Q took a long-term sponsorship of Channel 4’s home programming, 4Homes. Channel 4 got a committed partner for its property and home shows.
brought: Stores, products and a long-term sponsorship commitment.
The home and property shows that inspired people to start projects.
turning_point: Over three years the sponsorship repositioned B&Q with the customers it most needed, built on how people think about improving their homes.
measure: Incremental sales the IPA paper attributes to the campaign, as B&Q held its share in tough trading
evidence: The IPA paper credits the sponsorship with £233m of incremental sales over three years while B&Q maintained its share. That is a modelled estimate.
lesson: In a downturn, a long-term sponsorship can keep a brand in people’s plans until they are ready to spend.
take: The partnership that kept people dreaming about their homes when they couldn’t afford to act. Patience paid.

title: We All Make the Games
sector: Fast food and the Olympic Games
hook: A sponsor under fire made the Games about the public.
situation: McDonald’s sponsorship of the 2012 Olympic and Paralympic Games drew a storm of criticism. People questioned whether a fast food brand belonged at a sporting event.
exchange: McDonald’s paid to be an official partner of the Games. Instead of celebrating athletes, its campaign celebrated everyone who made the Games happen.
brought: Sponsorship money, restaurants and a nationwide campaign.
The biggest event in Britain for a generation.
turning_point: Leo Burnett’s ‘We all make the Games’ ran across many platforms and responded to the Games as they unfolded.
metric_label: Link with the Games, per the IPA paper
measure: The IPA paper reports the campaign persuaded people of a credible link between McDonald’s and the Games. Brand tracking, not sales
evidence: The IPA paper’s evidence is brand tracking that shows people came to accept the link. The summary doesn’t give a sales figure.
lesson: When people question why you are in a partnership, make it about them, not you.
take: The hardest brief in the edition: a sponsorship people didn’t want. The answer was to step back and let the public be the hero.

creative.label: Watch ‘We All Made the Games’ on Leo Burnett UK’s channel

title: Helping Men Look Good and Do Good
hook: A razor brand partnered with the charity that asks men to grow a moustache.
situation: Facial hair was in fashion, a problem for a brand built on the clean shave. Gillette was launching the ProGlide Styler, a trimmer made for moustaches.
exchange: Gillette backed Movember’s month of moustaches. Movember got a big partner, and Gillette got a reason for young men to buy a styler.
brought: A new trimmer, money and a national campaign.
A charity with a young, style-conscious following.
turning_point: Through Movember 2013 a campaign in press, outdoor, radio and events used a 1950s Gillette tone with modern slang.
measure: The ProGlide Styler’s ranking during the campaign, per the IPA paper, which also notes over £20m raised for men’s health
evidence: The IPA paper reports the styler became the top-selling razor across Movember. The £20m raised is Movember’s total for the period, not money from Gillette alone.
lesson: If a trend threatens your brand, partner with the people driving it rather than fighting it.
take: Clever and honest: Gillette admitted men weren’t shaving, and sold them the tool to look after the moustache instead.
credit: Abbott Mead Vickers BBDO for Gillette

creative.label: Watch a later Gillette UK Movember film on its channel

title: Christmas Is for Sharing
hook: A supermarket’s Christmas advert marked a hundred years since the First World War truce.
situation: Supermarkets compete hard at Christmas, and 2014 was a tough year. It was also the centenary of the 1914 Christmas truce.
exchange: Sainsbury’s made its Christmas film with the Royal British Legion, and sold products that raised money for the charity.
brought: Its Christmas advertising slot, stores and products.
Authority on the history, and a cause people trusted.
turning_point: The ‘Christmas Truce’ film ran in 2014, followed in 2015 by ‘Mog’s Christmas Calamity’ with Save the Children.
measure: Profit return on investment estimated in the IPA paper for the 2014 campaign
evidence: The IPA paper estimates a profit return of 24.34 for every 1 invested in 2014, and says the 2015 campaign paid back at least as much. Sainsbury’s outperformed its big four rivals in value and volume share.
lesson: A cause partner can give a brand permission to tell a story it couldn’t tell alone.
take: The partnership did what no supermarket could do alone: make a Christmas advert about history and be trusted for it.
credit: IPA 2016 · Silver · Abbott Mead Vickers BBDO for Sainsbury’s

title: At the Heart of T in the Park
hook: Possibly the world’s longest-running music sponsorship.
situation: Tennent’s is Scotland’s best-known beer brand. When a brand is everywhere, it risks being taken for granted.
exchange: Tennent’s sponsored the T in the Park festival, its initial in the name. In 2015 it refreshed the partnership with a new identity, brand experiences and apps.
brought: Long-term sponsorship and beer for every festival-goer.
Scotland’s biggest music festival and its crowds.
turning_point: The 2015 festival activity was designed to keep drinkers loyal and get non-drinkers of the brand to try it.
measure: The IPA paper reports sampling and sales above target for the 2015 activity. No figure is given in the summary
evidence: The IPA paper reports above-target sampling and sales, and more awareness of the sponsorship. The summary gives no number, so it counts as a sales trend.
lesson: Even a long sponsorship needs refreshing. Familiar can become invisible.
take: The partnership is so old the festival carries the beer’s initial. That is the dream outcome for any sponsor, and the risk too.

title: 44 Days of Crazy
data_source: Mastercard’s cards, the Rugby World Cup
hook: A payments company with no link to rugby turned fans’ passion into card spending.
situation: Mastercard sponsored the 2015 Rugby World Cup, but had little association with the sport. It wanted more card use during the tournament.
exchange: Mastercard paid to sponsor the tournament and ran its ‘Rugby-ification’ idea across search, social, transport hubs and media partnerships.
brought: Six weeks of fans, many of them visitors from abroad.
turning_point: Over the 44 days of the tournament, card use rose near venues and among overseas visitors, and more outlets started accepting Mastercard.
measure: Additional spending on Mastercard estimated in the IPA paper, with $700m of long-term incremental spending forecast
evidence: The IPA paper estimates $45m of extra purchasing and forecasts $700m over the long term. The forecast is a projection, not a measured result.
lesson: Measure a sponsorship on the behaviour it changes during the event, not just on awareness.
take: A sponsorship judged on transactions, not tickets. Mastercard knew what it wanted from the rugby, and counted it.

title: Don’t Watch Alone
data_source: Heineken’s beer, Europe’s biggest club competition
hook: A sponsor noticed fans drank more when they watched together, and built a campaign on it.
situation: Heineken’s Champions League sponsorship was well known, but sales growth was slowing. Fans were more likely to drink Heineken when they watched with others.
exchange: Heineken used its sponsorship to encourage social viewing, with José Mourinho as spokesman, high-impact TV and video, and personalised reminders.
brought: Sponsorship money and a global campaign.
Europe’s biggest club football, watched in pubs and homes.
turning_point: After the campaign, fans watched 20% fewer games alone, and Heineken’s sales rose in the markets where it ran.
metric_label: Year-on-year volume growth in campaign markets
measure: Volume growth in Champions League markets, against declines in countries without the campaign, per the IPA paper
evidence: The IPA paper compares markets with the campaign against those without, which works like a control group. It also reports a 5% rise in global brand penetration.
lesson: Use a sponsorship to change a behaviour that sells your product, not just to be seen next to the sport.
take: The second Heineken case in this archive, and the opposite of its Bond deal. Here the partnership had a job, and a measure.
credit: IPA 2018 · Silver · Publicis Italy for Heineken

creative.label: Watch ‘#ShareTheSofa for the UEFA Champions League’ on Heineken’s channel

brand: DFS × Team GB and British Heart Foundation
title: A Brand People Value
data_source: DFS’s sofas, Team GB and the BHF
hook: A sofa retailer known for sales used partnerships to be liked, not just bought.
situation: DFS needed more affluent sofa shoppers to hit its growth targets. It was famous for price offers, but not for being loved.
exchange: Alongside its advertising, DFS partnered with the British Heart Foundation and Team GB to build affection for the brand.
brought: Stores, sofas and a multi-year marketing budget.
National pride and a trusted cause.
turning_point: Over a multi-year strategy, the partnerships helped DFS appeal to the shoppers it had struggled to reach.
metric_label: Estimated incremental sales over six years
measure: Incremental sales estimated in the IPA paper, with a 64% rise in profit return
evidence: The IPA paper estimates £109m of incremental sales and a 64% increase in profit return, with consideration up 28% among more affluent shoppers. The partnerships were one part of a wider campaign, so their share can’t be separated out.
lesson: Partnerships can build the affection that price promotions can’t. Measure them as part of the whole plan.
take: Partnerships as one ingredient in a recipe, not the whole meal. That is how most of them work in real life.
credit: IPA 2018 · Gold · krow Communications and MediaCom for DFS

brand: Tourism Ireland × Game of Thrones and Derry Girls
title: Lights, Cameras, Collaboration
data_source: Tourism agencies, two hit TV shows
hook: Tourism agencies borrowed the magic of two TV shows without the rights to use them fully.
situation: Game of Thrones and Derry Girls were filmed in Northern Ireland and had made people want to visit. The tourism agencies didn’t have full rights to use the shows’ footage.
exchange: The agencies worked with the programme makers to create their own experiences, such as a Game of Thrones tapestry and TV sponsorship in the style of Derry Girls characters.
brought: Marketing budgets and the places themselves.
Stories, characters and fans around the world.
turning_point: The work ran as visitors returned after the pandemic, and aimed to turn viewers into visitors.
metric_label: Of Croatia in search interest, per the IPA paper
measure: Search volumes for Northern Ireland compared with Croatia, another Game of Thrones location, with improved consideration of Northern Ireland
evidence: The IPA paper compares search interest with Croatia and tracks consideration. That is a useful comparison, but it measures interest, not visits caused.
lesson: When you can’t license the content, partner with its makers to create something new around it.
take: A partnership built around a limitation. The tapestry exists because the rights didn’t, and it became a tourist attraction itself.
credit: IPA 2024 · Publicis London and OMD UK for Tourism Ireland

creative.label: Watch ‘The Stunning Game of Thrones Legacy Woven in Ireland’ on Discover Ireland’s channel
